notes: Fatah kept at 18 (ruling, MD). Coalition slot 19 holds the PDFLP (Hawatmeh), moved from MD slot 5 because MD's PPP did not exist in 1970 and the PDFLP fits independent Marxism; it keeps the MD DFLP sprite. Slot 5 = Wadie Haddad's PFLP External Operations apparatus. PFLP-GC fills slot 6 (replacing the anachronistic MD Qassam clique). Sa'iqa 7, ALF 21 and PLA 22 follow MD. Shia slots use the Shia refugees of the Seven Villages (8) and Khomeinist volunteers in Fatah camps (9). West Bank notables split: Ja'bari's Hebron (0), Nablus notables (1), Shehadeh's two-state circle (2), Hashemite loyalists (23).

0.name: Diwan al-Ja'bari
0.text:
The Ja'bari Court is the patronage machine of Sheikh Muhammad Ali al-Ja'bari, mayor of Hebron since 1948, several times a Jordanian minister and the most powerful notable of the southern West Bank. Since the June War he has dealt directly with the Israeli military government, floated plans for West Bank self-rule and treats the fedayeen as a threat to the order he has kept for two decades.

The Court stands for clan hierarchy, religious conservatism and accommodation with whichever power holds the land, preferring negotiated autonomy under Western patronage to revolutionary war. Its strength lies in Hebron's great families, the municipal payroll, the Shari'a courts and Ja'bari's personal channels to Amman and to the Israeli authorities.

1.name: A'yan Jabal Nablus
1.text:
The Notables of Jabal Nablus are the merchant and landowning families who have dominated the northern West Bank since Ottoman times, among them the Masris, Tuqans and Abd al-Hadis. Their senior figure is Hikmat al-Masri, a former speaker of the Jordanian House of Representatives. Under Israeli occupation since 1967, they keep municipal councils, chambers of commerce and the soap and olive trade running across the open bridges to Jordan.

Cautious and propertied, they want an end to occupation through diplomacy and Western goodwill rather than guerrilla war, and they fear both fedayeen reprisals and radical slogans. Their leverage is economic: credit, jobs, land and the export trade on which much of the West Bank lives.

2.name: Al-Kiyan al-Filastini
2.text:
The Palestinian Entity is the circle of West Bank lawyers, journalists and professionals who since 1967 have argued for a sovereign Palestinian state in the West Bank and Gaza living in peace beside Israel. Its best-known voice is the Ramallah lawyer Aziz Shehadeh, a refugee from Jaffa, joined by the Jerusalem journalist Muhammad Abu Shilbaya. Amman calls them separatists and the fedayeen call them defeatists.

They stand for a negotiated two-state settlement, the rule of law, elections and a free press, and look to the United States and Western Europe for guarantees. Their following is small but educated: Christian and Muslim professionals of Ramallah, Bethlehem and Jerusalem who doubt that armed struggle can ever win.

3.name: Al-Ittihad al-'Amm li-'Ummal Filastin
3.text:
The General Union of Palestinian Workers is the PLO's labour federation, founded in the early 1960s to organise a working class scattered by 1948: camp labourers in Lebanon and Syria, construction and oil workers in Kuwait and the Gulf, and wage earners in Jordan. Since the fedayeen organisations took over the PLO in 1969, Fatah cadres dominate its leadership.

The union campaigns for labour rights, social insurance and fair treatment of Palestinian migrants in host countries, and channels workers into the national movement through dues, strikes and solidarity funds. It favours a broad, socially minded nationalism over sectarian Marxism, and its leverage lies in the remittance economy that keeps the refugee camps alive.

4.name: Al-Jabha al-Sha'biyya li-Tahrir Filastin
4.english: Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine
4.text:
The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine was founded in December 1967 by George Habash, merging the Palestinian branch of the Arab Nationalist Movement with smaller commando groups. In February 1969 it formally adopted Marxism-Leninism. Based in Jordan's camps and cities, it is Fatah's most prominent rival, famous for the airliner hijackings planned by Wadie Haddad.

The Front holds that Palestine will be liberated only through a people's war that also topples the 'reactionary' Arab regimes, above all the Hashemite throne. It denounces American imperialism and Zionism, admires Vietnam, China and Cuba and seeks Soviet-bloc support. Its base is refugee youth, students and intellectuals, and its leverage is discipline and spectacular violence.
4.wiki: Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine

5.name: Al-Jabha al-Sha'biyya li-Tahrir Filastin – al-'Amaliyyat al-Kharijiyya
5.native_full: Al-Jabha al-Sha'biyya li-Tahrir Filastin – al-'Amaliyyat al-Kharijiyya
5.text:
PFLP External Operations is the secret apparatus run by Dr. Wadie Haddad, Habash's oldest comrade, to carry the war beyond the Middle East. Since 1968 it has diverted an El Al airliner to Algiers, attacked Israeli aircraft at Athens and Zurich and, in August 1969, seized TWA Flight 840 with Leila Khaled among the hijackers. It answers to Haddad more than to the Front's congress.

Haddad's doctrine is to pursue the enemy everywhere: strike Israel's airlines, its Western patrons and their economic interests until the world cannot ignore Palestine. The apparatus scorns mass politics and programmes and recruits a small elite of operatives and foreign sympathisers. Its leverage is fear, headlines and freedom from any Arab state's control.
5.wiki: Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine – External Operations

6.name: Al-Jabha al-Sha'biyya li-Tahrir Filastin – al-Qiyada al-'Amma
6.english: Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine – General Command
6.native_full: Al-Jabha al-Sha'biyya li-Tahrir Filastin – al-Qiyada al-'Amma
6.text:
The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine – General Command split from Habash's Front in 1968 under Ahmed Jibril, a former Syrian army officer who had founded the Palestine Liberation Front earlier in the decade. Small, tightly drilled and based in Syria and Jordan, it prides itself on technical skill with explosives and long-range operations.

The General Command rejects ideological debate as a distraction: fighting comes first, and Marxist theorising is for intellectuals. It is hardline, authoritarian and anti-Western, aligned with Damascus and open to any patron who supplies arms, from the Soviet bloc to radical Arab regimes. Its leverage lies in Syrian protection, a professional cadre and its readiness to wreck any compromise.
6.wiki: Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine – General Command

7.name: Tala'i' Harb al-Tahrir al-Sha'biyya – Quwwat al-Sa'iqa
7.native_full: Tala'i' Harb al-Tahrir al-Sha'biyya – Quwwat al-Sa'iqa
7.text:
As-Sa'iqa, formally the Vanguards of the Popular Liberation War, is the Palestinian fedayeen force of Syria's ruling Ba'ath Party, built up since 1966 from refugees in Syria and armed and paid by Damascus. It is the second-largest guerrilla organisation after Fatah and holds seats on the PLO Executive Committee.

Its programme is Ba'athist: Palestine is part of the Arab nation, and its liberation must serve Arab unity and socialism under Ba'athist leadership. Sa'iqa follows the radical Syrian line of Salah Jadid, hostile to the West and close to Moscow, and acts as Damascus's lever inside the PLO. Its leverage is Syrian money, territory and guns; its weakness is that it can never act alone.

8.name: Ahl al-Qura al-Sab'
8.text:
The People of the Seven Villages are the Shia Palestinians of Upper Galilee, driven out in 1948 from Hunin, Qadas, al-Malikiyya, Tarbikha, Saliha, al-Nabi Yusha' and Abil al-Qamh. Most now live in Tyre, the Beirut suburbs and the camps of southern Lebanon, stateless and caught between Palestinian and Lebanese identities. Imam Musa al-Sadr, head of the new Supreme Islamic Shia Council, courts them.

Their notables and young clerics want Shia dignity within the Palestinian cause: recognition, education, welfare and a return to the Galilee. They reject sectarian isolation but distrust secular Marxists, and lean toward Fatah's pragmatism. Their leverage is a bridge position between the fedayeen and Lebanon's awakening Shia community.

9.name: Ansar Khumayni
9.text:
Khomeini's Partisans are Iranian and Arab Shia militants who have found their way to Fatah training camps in Jordan and Lebanon, convinced that the war against Israel and the struggle against the Shah are one. Their inspiration is Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, in exile in Najaf, who in 1968 allowed religious dues to be spent on the fedayeen.

They seek an Islamic revolution led by the clergy, the overthrow of the Shah and the liberation of Jerusalem, and despise both American power and Soviet atheism. Few in number, they learn guerrilla skills from secular Palestinians while preaching against secularism. Their leverage lies in mosque networks, clerical funds and the prestige of joining Palestine's armed struggle.

10.name: Al-Hay'a al-Islamiyya al-'Ulya
10.text:
The Higher Islamic Council was formed by Jerusalem's ulama in July 1967 to keep the city's Islamic courts, endowments and holy places outside Israeli law after annexation. Its first head, Sheikh Abd al-Hamid al-Sa'ih, was deported to Jordan that September; Sheikh Hilmi al-Muhtasib now leads it. Since the arson at al-Aqsa Mosque in August 1969 it has spoken for Muslim outrage worldwide.

The Council is conservative and legalist, upholding the Shari'a, the waqf and Jordanian religious authority, and it is paid and protected by the Hashemite crown. It shuns guerrilla politics but refuses any recognition of occupation. Its leverage lies in al-Aqsa, the Friday pulpit and the endowments that support schools, clinics and clerics.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Liberation Party, was founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the Shari'a judge Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani, who now directs it from Beirut. Banned in Jordan and throughout the region, it works through secret study cells among students, teachers and officers, and its supporters have been arrested for coup plots in Amman.

The party teaches that Palestine and every Muslim land can only be freed by restoring a single Islamic caliphate, to be won by persuading army officers to hand it power. It rejects nationalism, parliaments, the fedayeen organisations and both Washington and Moscow. Its leverage is ideological discipline and patient infiltration of the security forces.

12.name: Jama'at al-Ikhwan al-Muslimin fi Filastin
12.text:
The Muslim Brotherhood in Palestine has had branches in Gaza and the West Bank since the 1940s. Crushed in Gaza by Nasser's police, it is rebuilding under Israeli occupation through preachers such as the paralysed teacher Sheikh Ahmed Yassin, while its West Bank members belong to the legal Jordanian Brotherhood. Brotherhood volunteers fight from their own 'Sheikhs' Camps' in Jordan under Fatah's umbrella.

The Brotherhood holds that liberation must follow the re-Islamisation of society: mosques, schools, charity and moral discipline come before guns. It rejects secular nationalism and Marxism, distrusts the PLO and keeps a cautious modus vivendi with King Hussein. Its leverage lies in mosques, welfare work and patient grassroots organisation.

13.name: Jihaz al-Rasd
13.text:
Rasd is Fatah's intelligence and security service, created after the 1967 war under Salah Khalaf (Abu Iyad), with Ali Hassan Salameh among its leading officers. Operating from Amman, it vets recruits, hunts informers, watches rival organisations and liaises with Arab intelligence services from Cairo to Algiers.

The apparatus is pragmatic rather than ideological: it serves the unity of the revolution and Arafat's leadership, and values order, secrecy and loyalty above slogans. It keeps aloof from both blocs while dealing with anyone useful, and prepares the movement for open conflict with the Jordanian state should it come. Its leverage lies in files, informants and men trained to act without asking questions.

14.name: Al-Hay'a al-'Arabiyya al-'Ulya
14.text:
The Arab Higher Committee was formed in 1936 to lead the Palestinian Arab revolt and remains the vehicle of Hajj Amin al-Husseini, former Mufti of Jerusalem, now living in Lebanon. Eclipsed since 1964 by the PLO, it survives as a small office of veteran politicians, Husseini clan loyalists and religious notables.

The Committee speaks for the Palestinian nationalism of the Mandate era: Islamic, conservative, anti-Zionist and anti-communist. It distrusts the Hashemites who annexed the West Bank, keeps ties to Saudi Arabia and conservative Gulf patrons, and views the Marxist fedayeen with alarm. Its leverage is the Mufti's lingering prestige among older refugees and village elders.

15.name: Al-Bank al-'Arabi
15.text:
The Arab Bank was founded in Jerusalem in 1930 by Abdul Hameed Shoman, a self-made Palestinian financier, and moved its headquarters to Amman after 1948. Still chaired by Shoman, it is one of the largest Arab-owned private banks, with branches from Beirut to the Gulf and deep roots in the Palestinian diaspora.

The bank stands for Palestinian enterprise, sound money and the commercial networks that link exiles across the Arab world. It avoids open politics, quietly finances national institutions and prefers stability to revolution, wary of any upheaval in Jordan or Lebanon that could threaten its deposits. Its leverage lies in capital, credit and the savings of hundreds of thousands of Palestinian families.

16.name: Sharikat Ittihad al-Muqawilin
16.text:
Consolidated Contractors Company was founded in Beirut in 1952 by Hasib Sabbagh and Said Khoury, refugees from Palestine, and has grown into one of the largest construction firms of the Arab world, building pipelines, roads and ports for oil companies and Gulf governments. Its offices employ thousands of Palestinian engineers and technicians.

CCC embodies the diaspora's self-made, pragmatic bourgeoisie: it believes in private enterprise, open markets, professional education and Western contracts, and fears that revolution will close Gulf doors to Palestinians. Sabbagh funds schools, scholarships and moderate nationalists. Its leverage lies in contracts, jobs and the respect of conservative Arab rulers.

17.name: Al-Mashru' al-Insha'i al-'Arabi
17.text:
The Arab Development Society was founded in 1945 by Musa Alami, a Jerusalem lawyer and veteran nationalist. Since 1949 it has turned a stretch of barren land near Jericho into a farm and vocational school for refugee boys, proving that fresh water lay beneath the Jordan Valley desert. Damaged in the June War, the farm carries on under occupation.

The Society believes in reclaiming the land through wells, irrigation, tree planting and soil care, so that Palestinians stay rooted on their own soil rather than in camps. It is non-partisan, distrustful of slogans and supported by Western donors. Its leverage is moral: a model of self-reliance and stewardship that admirers across the Arab world cite.

18.name: Harakat al-Tahrir al-Watani al-Filastini
18.text:
Fatah, the Palestinian National Liberation Movement, was founded in Kuwait in the late 1950s by Yasser Arafat, Khalil al-Wazir, Salah Khalaf and others, and launched its armed struggle on 1 January 1965. After the Battle of Karameh in March 1968 it became the largest fedayeen organisation, and in February 1969 Arafat was elected Chairman of the PLO Executive Committee.

Fatah's creed is simple: Palestinians must liberate Palestine themselves through armed struggle, without waiting for Arab regimes and without meddling in their affairs; it now proposes a democratic, secular state for Muslims, Christians and Jews. Non-aligned, it takes arms from China and Algeria and money from the Gulf. Its leverage is mass support in the camps.

19.name: Al-Jabha al-Sha'biyya al-Dimuqratiyya li-Tahrir Filastin
19.english: Popular Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine
19.text:
The Popular Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine broke away from Habash's Popular Front in February 1969, led by Nayef Hawatmeh, a Jordanian-born Christian and former Arab Nationalist Movement cadre. Small but intellectually energetic, it is based in Jordan and draws on students, teachers and young camp activists.

The Democratic Front is the resistance's independent Marxist pole, inspired by Vietnam, China and Cuba rather than Moscow's orthodoxy. It calls for popular councils in Jordan, attacks petty-bourgeois nationalism and is the first to propose a democratic state in which Arabs and Jews live as equals, reaching out to anti-Zionist Israeli leftists. Its leverage lies in ideas, cadres and influence over Fatah's left.
19.wiki: Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine

20.name: Munazzamat Filastin al-'Arabiyya
20.text:
The Arab Palestine Organization was formed in 1969 by Ahmad Za'rur and other fighters who left the Popular Front when it embraced Marxism. Small and loosely organised, it operates from Jordan and enjoys Egyptian sympathy.

It preaches a plain, emotional nationalism: Palestine is Arab, the fedayeen are its heroes, and ideologies imported from Moscow or Peking only divide the people. It distrusts intellectuals and party theorists, attacks the bureaucrats of the big organisations and calls on the masses to rally behind fighters, faith and Arab honour. Its leverage is its appeal to young refugees and villagers who feel neither Marxist nor Ba'athist, and Cairo's indulgence.

21.name: Jabhat al-Tahrir al-'Arabiyya
21.text:
The Arab Liberation Front was established in April 1969 by the Iraqi wing of the Ba'ath Party as its own fedayeen organisation, a riposte to Syria's as-Sa'iqa. Its fighters are recruited in Iraq and among Palestinians loyal to Baghdad, and its leadership answers to the Ba'ath command around President Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr and Saddam Hussein.

The Front insists that Palestine is an Arab cause rather than a Palestinian one, and that its liberation demands the unity of the Arab nation under Ba'athist leadership. It is militaristic, ultranationalist and authoritarian, hostile to the West and to Palestinian particularism alike. Its leverage lies in Iraqi money and the Iraqi troops stationed in Jordan.

22.name: Jaysh al-Tahrir al-Filastini
22.text:
The Palestine Liberation Army is the regular force created by the PLO in 1964, organised in brigades stationed in host countries: Ain Jalut in Egypt, Hittin in Syria and Qadisiyya alongside the Iraqi forces. Since 1968 it has also fielded the Popular Liberation Forces, its own commando arm in the occupied territories.

Its officers are trained soldiers who see a disciplined army, not scattered guerrilla bands, as the core of a future Palestinian state. Yet their units are paid and in practice commanded by their hosts, and the PLA command repeatedly clashes with the fedayeen leadership over authority. Its leverage lies in heavy weapons, formal military rank and the backing of Arab general staffs.

23.name: Wahdat al-Daffatayn
23.text:
Unity of the Two Banks is the camp of West Bank notables, officials and families who remain loyal to King Hussein and to the 1950 union of the West Bank with Jordan. Its leading figure is Anwar al-Khatib, the Jordanian governor of Jerusalem in 1967, alongside former ministers, judges and mayors who still draw salaries from Amman.

The loyalists want the West Bank restored to the Hashemite kingdom through Western and United Nations diplomacy under Resolution 242, and see the fedayeen as a danger to the crown. Conservative, propertied and anti-communist, they depend on Jordanian patronage, passports and the open bridges. Their leverage is the state machinery Amman still runs in the occupied territories.
